A RISK WITHOUT A COUNTERMEASURE IS A BLOCKER.
that is the DEFAULT — so silence stops the work

ACCEPTED UNKNOWN is a blocker accepted without
even knowing its size — allowed, never by default.

an unmarked temporary countermeasure is a
MACHINE: nothing merely NAMED. every risk proven, measured and given a
likelihood, or an explicit accepted unknown. impact and value
in comparable units. every countermeasure states its expected
effect. every TEMPORARY one carries its return condition.
HUMAN: Tony accepts each blocker BY NAME — including the unknowns and
any low-likelihood fatal. rounding a small probability to zero
silently is exactly what this gate exists to stop.
HIGH IMPACT + HIGH LIKELIHOOD + NO COUNTERMEASURE
= DEAD PROJECT. not a kill you choose — a state you
recognise. the thing is already dead; the only
question is how long before someone says so.
THIS IS THE LIMIT ON ACCEPTANCE. every other blocker
can be accepted by name. this one cannot, or
'accept by name' becomes an escape hatch for
anything. the only moves left are RESHAPE — change
the thing so the risk is no longer fatal — or KILL.
a kill here is a SUCCESS: it is the cheapest place
carries the surviving risks and their countermeasures forward. design
builds AROUND them — a countermeasure is a constraint on the shape,
not a note in a document nobody opens.
OPEN on this stage — accepted risks age, and nothing brings them back.
A TEMPORARY countermeasure is self-expiring: it carries its own return condition, so that class is answered.
The other two are not. An ACCEPTED UNKNOWN was accepted because evidence was too expensive — evidence gets
cheaper. A LOW-LIKELIHOOD FATAL was accepted at one moment's odds — odds move. Today both are permanent by
default, which is the same shape as the design doc that held the answer and went unread: right when decided,
